The legal age for marriage in the United States is not uniform and varies by state [d1]. The general standard, as established by the 1970 Uniform Marriage and Divorce Act, sets the presumptive age of consent at 18, but 16- and 17-year-olds can still marry with parental or judicial permission in many states [d8]. As of recent data, child marriage remains legal in 37 US states, with only 13 states (including Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and Vermont) having set the minimum marriage age at 18 with no exceptions, while 20 states have no minimum age requirement at all when a parental or judicial waiver is obtained [d6]. In states like New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Minnesota, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Virginia, New Hampshire, Washington State, Michigan, and Vermont, minors under 18 cannot marry under any circumstance [d9]. Massachusetts, for example, previously had no statutory minimum marriage age, but in 2022 Governor Charlie Baker signed a law raising the legal marriage age to 18 with no exceptions, making it the 7th state to end child marriage [d5]. Globally, the marriageable age also varies widely, with some countries setting different ages for males and females and allowing exceptions with parental consent [d9].
